doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Saxophone, drums and the Army band
summary: He tries alto sax, learns drums from a friend, finds asymmetrical jazz drumming hard, and plays trap drums in the Army band.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: So I played that a little bit, didn’t really like it, and didn’t have an opportunity to get into any music on it, because the stuff we were playing, the parts weren’t very interesting. And by this time I’d become interested in jazz. And in high school this same teacher had formed a little swing band, played stocks and was trying to teach us how that idiom went. So I’d bring my baritone horn to rehearsal and say where are the baritone horn parts? And again I was crushed to discover that they didn’t write for that instrument. So I fooled around the last year of high school. I tried saxophone for a while because my older brother had an old Buescher alto that he’d left behind when he went in the Navy, and I never got a good sound on that. And when some better — I guess I started that in my junior year. And when some better saxophones came into the band I was aced out immediately. But the drummer had graduated so I ran over to the service station where he worked and said, “Show me that thing you play on the hi-hat,” and, “how do you do this” and “what are the basic things you need to know about drumming?” I could hear what the drummers had been doing, and I did that well enough. I was a fairly decent drummer because I could keep time. But when it got into really being a jazz drummer later on, I © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

had trouble with I wanted everything to be symmetrical, and jazz players have to be able to keep the time going with one hand while they do other things with their other hands. And I always wanted to do things that were symmetrical, and I couldn’t get the asymmetrical things to work right for me. So I eventually gave up drums just by default, but I played them, oh, through high school and in college a little bit. And when I got in the Army, all the drummers in the band I finally got into as a baritone player, were street drummers. So when we would have club dates and service club jobs for dancing, I would be the trap drummer. I met a cornet player from Brookline, Massachusetts in the Army who was a real moldy fig in those days. He loved everything from Louis Armstrong up to about Mugsy Spanier.
